title: Remembering the pre-Google web, when search was an experiment
gist: An oral-history of 1990s web search argues that AltaVista, Lycos, Excite, HotBot, Yahoo and Ask Jeeves were not failed precursors but competing bets on how discovery should work — human directories, raw crawl scale, portals, or natural language — and that Google won by fusing link-based authority (PageRank), a stripped-down utility interface, and scale at the exact moment the web outgrew human curation. The implicit warning is that discovery interfaces are historically contingent and have flipped before, and that ranking incentives reshape what content gets made at all.

insights.claim: In the mid-1990s web, search engines were only one channel of discovery alongside Yahoo-style directories, bookmarks, newsgroups, email signatures and site-to-site links, because the web was still small enough that human organization could compete with machine indexing.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Discovery share is not a law of nature — whenever content volume outruns whatever the incumbent index can rank, alternative channels regain share; a useful lens for judging AI-answer vs. link-search displacement today.
insights.quote: Search engines existed, but they were only one part of a larger ecosystem that blended curation and accident.
insights.locator: A different kind of web

insights.claim: Usenet, conceived in 1979, trained an entire generation to navigate online information through topic categories and communities rather than a single query box, establishing discovery habits years before commercial web search engines existed.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Community-mediated discovery predates and outlived algorithmic search — relevant to valuing Reddit/forum-style properties as durable, non-index-dependent traffic sources.
insights.quote: It was the way to find out about websites that might interest you
insights.locator: Before those engines became the main public interface

insights.claim: Webrings functioned as a decentralized, trust-based distribution network in which site owners embedded a code block linking to the next related site and a volunteer curator controlled the sequence, with participants not even considering the possibility of sabotage.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Distribution systems built on assumed good faith scale only until the payoff for gaming them exceeds the cost — the same failure curve now facing open-web crawling and AI training data.
insights.quote: You’d get a block of code and put it on the bottom of your site’s HTML page, and it would embed a link to the next website related to this one.
insights.locator: Then a couple of years later, webrings popped up

insights.claim: Yahoo began as a human-edited, nested subject directory in which real editors vetted submissions for legitimacy and importance, making directory acceptance a scarce distribution asset that agencies treated as the highlight of a client launch.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Gatekept, editorially scarce placement historically commanded premium value; watch for the same dynamic returning wherever AI answer engines whitelist a limited set of trusted sources.
insights.quote: Yahoo was like the Yellow Pages, but only for websites.
insights.locator: Directories before algorithms

insights.claim: Yahoo's editorial gatekeeping was arbitrary enough that a regional American Cancer Society branch site was rejected as 'not significant enough,' with the reviewer suggesting it get linked from a national ACS page that did not yet exist.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Human review is not automatically higher quality than algorithmic ranking — a caution against assuming manual curation solves the trust problem in AI-era content ranking.
insights.quote: They recommended we contact the main ACS and have them link the site from their page… that they didn’t have yet.
insights.locator: I remember one time submitting the website

insights.claim: Human curation of the web was doomed by unit economics rather than quality: it became more expensive and less timely as page count ballooned, and the moment pages outnumbered the people who could classify them, crawlers and ranking systems inherited the category.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: The cost-per-item-curated versus items-created ratio is the governing variable in any discovery business — apply it directly to moderation, app stores, and AI-generated content floods.
insights.quote: The moment the number of pages outstripped the number of people who could reasonably classify them, the future belonged to crawlers and ranking systems.
insights.locator: But the model had obvious limits

themes.theme: Crawl scale and the speed expectation

insights.claim: AltaVista's advance was pairing a fast crawler with scalable indexing software, and it was already handling millions of HTTP requests per day shortly after launch, converting search from catalog browsing into querying a giant machine.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Infrastructure throughput, not interface polish, was the first moat in search — the same argument now made for inference capacity in AI answer products.
insights.quote: It made search feel less like browsing a catalog and more like querying a giant machine.
insights.locator: The rise of crawlers

insights.claim: AltaVista lost the search market but permanently reset user expectations that search must be immediate, and once users experienced fast sweeps of a huge index they stopped accepting sluggish, partial systems.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Category-defining products often capture the standard, not the profit — a template for judging today's first-movers whose main legacy may be raising the baseline for a later winner.
insights.quote: AltaVista didn’t win the search war, but it clarified the rules of engagement.
insights.locator: AltaVista’s moment

insights.claim: Early recall without precision was itself the failure mode: a specific question typed into AltaVista would routinely return roughly 40,000 results, leaving the user no better informed than before.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Index breadth without a ranking signal is worthless — the argument for why retrieval quality, not corpus size, is the binding constraint in retrieval-augmented systems.
insights.quote: You’d receive 40,000 results that would leave you just as confused as shouting into a crowded room.
insights.locator: Most people have completely forgotten how chaotic it really was

insights.claim: HotBot's technical credibility came from Inktomi's scalable backend, and its era marked the point where users began distinguishing index size from ranking sophistication as separate quality inputs.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: The search stack split early into crawl/index infrastructure versus ranking IP — a reminder that value in a discovery stack can sit in an invisible supplier layer.
insights.locator: HotBot, Inktomi, and technical credibility

themes.theme: Portal vs. utility: two interface bets

insights.claim: Lycos and Excite deliberately bundled search with news, email, sports, weather and finance channels to retain users on-site rather than send them off to results pages, treating search as a destination business instead of a routing utility.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: The engagement-maximizing portal model and the fastest-exit utility model are opposing monetization strategies; the utility model won search but the portal logic later returned in social feeds and AI chat.
insights.quote: They were search brands, but they were also portals, meaning they strove to be destinations as much as tools.
insights.locator: Lycos, Excite, and the portal era

insights.claim: The 'search engine' label in the 1990s covered wildly different products — directory services, pure crawlers, and portals with search bolted on as a tertiary feature — showing the category was completely unsettled rather than converging.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Label homogeneity hides business-model divergence in emerging categories — apply skepticism to any peer group currently lumped together as 'AI assistants'.
insights.locator: These companies demonstrated how unsettled the category was

insights.claim: Ask Jeeves attempted a conversational, natural-language query interface decades before large language models, and failed because users asked messy questions and the underlying systems could not infer intent reliably at scale.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: The interface idea was right and only the substrate was missing — evidence that today's LLM chat interfaces are the delayed completion of a 1990s product thesis, not a novel one.
insights.quote: Ask Jeeves was memorable because, without the underpinning of deep learning and LLMs, it purported to understand the user experience better than the technology of the time could support.
insights.locator: Ask Jeeves and the question interface

themes.theme: The manipulation arms race that created SEO

insights.claim: Early engines that leaned on on-page textual signals were trivially gamed by keyword stuffing, meaning marketing budgets could directly overpower content quality in rankings before the term 'search engine optimization' existed in its modern sense.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Any ranking signal computed from author-controlled inputs will be captured by advertisers — the structural argument for why AI systems must rank on signals the content owner cannot set.
insights.quote: If an engine relied mostly on easily manipulated on-page signals, marketing could overpower quality.
insights.locator: That tension exposed a weakness

insights.claim: Hiding keywords as white text on a white background was a mainstream, penalty-free webmaster tactic until engines began classifying it as spamdexing and acting on it in the late 1990s.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Enforcement lags exploitation by years in every ranking system — expect a comparable multi-year window of unpenalized AI-answer gaming before platforms respond.
insights.quote: There was no fear of penalties, and you built a website, crossed your fingers, and hoped for the best.
insights.locator: Search before SEO

insights.claim: The dominance of scraping and ranking converted the Internet into a content manufacturing facility, shifting websites from being written for people to being written primarily for search engine crawlers.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Whoever controls ranking controls what content gets produced at all — the mechanism by which an AI-answer layer could restructure the entire publishing supply chain a second time.
insights.quote: Websites went from being written for people to being written primarily for search engine crawlers.
insights.locator: The hard truth that most people do not want to face

insights.claim: Once search became the main gateway to the web, the previously experimental and testable publisher-engine feedback loop collapsed into an adversarial one, with professionalized departments guessing at ephemeral and mysterious ranking signals.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Gatekeeper opacity is a deliberate anti-gaming feature, and it creates a permanent, rent-extracting consultancy industry around every dominant discovery platform.
insights.locator: Once search became the main gateway to the web

insights.claim: Google's decisive contribution was changing the logic of ranking rather than inventing search: PageRank treated inbound links as authority signals, making relevance a function of how the web itself pointed at a page and thereby raising the cost of manipulation.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Durable ranking moats come from off-page signals the publisher cannot self-declare — the key test to apply to any new discovery or recommendation system.
insights.quote: Google’s crucial contribution was not that it discovered search; it was that it changed the logic of ranking.
insights.locator: PageRank changes everything

insights.claim: Google reinforced its ranking advantage with a stripped-down interface and a results page that got out of the way, deliberately positioning search as a utility rather than a portal amusement park.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Minimizing time-on-site beat maximizing it in this category — a direct challenge to engagement-optimized AI interfaces that reintroduce portal economics.
insights.quote: In practice, Google made the search box feel like the front door to the whole web
insights.locator: Just as importantly, Google paired that ranking approach

insights.claim: Google's win required the simultaneous combination of technical ranking, usability and scale arriving exactly when the rest of the Internet was ready to abandon the old order, implying timing rather than any single capability was decisive.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Single-factor explanations of platform dominance underprice the timing variable; the corollary is that a comparable readiness window is what a Google challenger would need.
insights.quote: Google won by combining technical rank, usability, and scale at exactly the moment the rest of the Internet was ready to abandon the old order.
insights.locator: Why the old web mattered

insights.claim: The pre-Google era supported more competing theories of how information should be found, categorized and judged — some trusting people, some crawlers, some directories, some plain-English questions — which means the current single-interface equilibrium was never inevitable.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: The strongest implied claim in the piece: search's dominant form is contingent and reversible, which is the bull case for any AI-native discovery challenger to an incumbent index.
insights.quote: That diversity is worth remembering because it shows that search was never necessarily destined to look the way it does now.
insights.locator: That diversity is worth remembering

insights.claim: The nostalgia for the pre-Google web is specifically for hand-built artisanal content and serendipitous multi-hop browsing paths, not for better retrieval quality, which the article concedes was slower, messier and less efficient.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Consumer appetite for serendipity and human-made content is a real but separate demand vector from retrieval efficiency — the addressable market for curation and 'human-made' provenance products.
insights.quote: It was made by real people using text editors such as Notepad and Dreamweaver.
insights.locator: The Internet contained an inherent level of clutter and chaos
